text.en: On a clear night we see thousands of stars. Some form patterns. Some wander across the sky. What are they and how far do they go? Let us look beyond Earth.

Stars are huge balls of hot gas that give out their own light. The Sun is a star, the nearest one to us. Stars look tiny because they are very far away. Constellations have recognisable star patterns. The seven stars called Saptarishi form part of Ursa Major, the Great Bear. Orion is another constellation. From places in the Northern Hemisphere where the Pole Star is visible, it appears almost fixed above the northern horizon and can help you find north.
Over one night, most stars seem to cross the sky because Earth spins. Earth turns beneath the changing view. Planets in our sky reflect sunlight. They often twinkle less than stars, although twinkling alone is not a sure way to identify a planet.
The solar system is the Sun with the planets and other objects that go around it. The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The four inner planets are rocky. Jupiter and Saturn are giants of gas. Moons orbit planets, and Earth has one Moon. There are also dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
Our solar system is part of a huge galaxy of stars called the Milky Way. There are billions of galaxies in the universe, and the universe is vast beyond imagination.

Picture two identical lamps. The nearer one looks larger to you. Distance has a similar effect in the sky. The Sun looks much larger than other stars because it is much nearer to Earth.
On a northern-sky chart, find Saptarishi, a pattern that looks like a bowl with a handle. The stars at the outer edge of the bowl can guide you toward the Pole Star.

board.text: Look along the bowl’s outer edge

text.en: Trace a line through the two stars along the outer edge of the bowl, away from its base and out past its open rim. That direction points you toward Polaris, the Pole Star.

board.text: Outer bowl stars → direction toward Polaris

text.en: On another sky chart, look for the three stars that appear in a row across Orion. The row is called Orion’s Belt. A chart helps you use this pattern even if the sky view is turned at an angle.

board.text: Find the three stars of Orion’s Belt

text.en: Extend the belt line on the chart in the direction of Sirius. Sirius is a bright star in a different constellation. A sky chart shows which way along the row to look.

board.text: Orion’s Belt can guide you toward Sirius

text.en: Stars in a pattern may actually lie at very different distances from Earth. The pattern records the directions in which we see them, like objects lined up in a picture from one viewpoint.

board.text: Pattern shows directions in Earth’s sky

text.en: Choose a safe place with an adult and look at the sky after dark. Mark the direction, date and time. A chart for that place and time helps you recognise patterns even when nearby buildings hide part of the sky.

board.text: Record location, direction, date and time

text.en: Compare two sketches made from the same spot an hour apart. Stars can shift compared with the top of a building, while their pattern stays much the same. Choose one landmark to line up the two sketches.

board.text: Compare the position of the pattern

text.en: Keep a daytime sky activity on the chart or model. Never stare at the Sun. Keep binoculars and telescopes pointed well away from it.

board.text: Keep viewing tools pointed away from the Sun

text.en: Trace Earth on a simple solar-system diagram. It turns around its own axis and also follows a path around the Sun. The path followed around another body is an orbit.
Count the first four planets from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. These have rocky surfaces. The gaps and sizes on our classroom sketch are simplified so the labels fit.

board.text: Four inner planets with rocky surfaces
Classroom sketch is not to scale

text.en: Continue past Mars to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are the two planets called ice giants.
A moon orbits a planet. Earth has one Moon and many other planets have moons as well. Follow the Moon around Earth, then follow Earth around the Sun to see how the two paths differ.

India’s Chandrayaan Three mission used the Vikram lander and the Pragyan rover to study the Moon. The lander touched down gently in twenty twenty-three, and the rover then moved onto the lunar surface.
On the map, the asteroid belt lies between the paths of Mars and Jupiter. It contains many rocky bodies. A comet contains ice, dust and rock and may grow a tail when it comes near the Sun.

board.text: Asteroid belt: between Mars and Jupiter
Comet near the Sun may grow a tail

text.en: Pluto belongs to the solar system and is classified as a dwarf planet. An object can orbit the Sun and belong to the solar system even though it is outside the list of eight planets.

board.text: The solar system includes more than planets

text.en: Zoom out in four stages. Start at Earth, find the solar system around the Sun, then find the Milky Way galaxy that contains our solar system. The universe contains the Milky Way and other galaxies.
A friend says the solar system and the Milky Way are the same size. On the board, point to the label that includes many stars, and explain where our Sun fits.

problem.en: Which planet is third from the Sun?

text.en: Order is Mercury, Venus, Earth.
Earth is third.

prompt.en: Explain why the Sun looks bigger than other stars.

requiredIdeas.en: Other stars are very much farther away.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking planets make their own light.
Thinking the Moon is a star.

points.en: There are eight planets in the solar system.
The Milky Way is our galaxy.
